summary: Defines an SMTP extension that lets a client name the responsible submitter of a message, meaning the address of the entity that most recently introduced it into the mail stream. Receiving servers can use that to decide whether the client may send for that domain. It was experimental and is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: Each letter gets a note saying who last handed it to the mail system, so the receiving post office can check that person really may send it.

subtitle: An SMTP extension to identify the party responsible for submitting a message

tldr.problem: When mail passes through multiple servers or forwarding services, it is hard for receivers to know who is actually responsible for introducing it into the mail system, making it easy to forge the sender's identity.
tldr.mechanism: This extension adds a SUBMITTER parameter to the SMTP MAIL command, allowing the sending client to specify the email address of the entity most recently responsible for submitting the message.
tldr.outcome: Receiving servers can validate the SUBMITTER domain against the connecting client before accepting the full message, catching spoofed mail earlier and more efficiently.

today: RFC 4405 is Historic. It was one of several experimental approaches to email sender authentication published by the MARID working group in 2006. The IESG noted at the time that there was no general technical consensus, and the community was invited to observe the success or failure of these approaches. Other mechanisms like SPF and DKIM eventually became more widely adopted.

sections.title: The Problem of Spoofing
sections.content:
Email spoofing—falsifying the sender's identity—is a common tactic for sending spam and phishing attacks. The challenge is determining who is actually responsible for submitting a message into the mail system, especially when messages are forwarded, relayed through multiple servers, or sent through a service on behalf of someone else.

There are two possible approaches: checking the SMTP protocol data (fast, but prone to false positives) or examining email headers (more accurate, but requires parsing the entire message). This extension tries to combine the benefits of both approaches.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes bad people send emails pretending to be someone else. This rule helps the mail system figure out who really sent it by marking each letter with who handed it over.

sections.title: The SUBMITTER Extension
sections.content:
The SUBMITTER extension adds an optional parameter to the MAIL command in SMTP. The parameter carries the email address of the entity most recently responsible for submitting the message, called the Purported Responsible Address (PRA). This is distinct from the MAIL FROM address, which is used for bounce messages and may differ.

An SMTP server that supports the extension advertises SUBMITTER in its EHLO response. The client includes the SUBMITTER parameter on messages it sends, allowing the server to extract the domain and validate whether the connecting client is authorized to send mail on behalf of that domain.
sections.plainLanguage: The client tells the server the address of whoever handed the letter to it. The server can then check if that person is allowed to send mail from that domain.

sections.title: How the SUBMITTER Parameter Works
sections.content:
The syntax is MAIL FROM:<alice@example.com> SUBMITTER=bob@almamater.edu, where characters like spaces and equals signs are encoded using xtext if needed. The SUBMITTER value must always contain the Purported Responsible Address derived from the message's RFC 2822 headers.

A receiving server SHOULD extract the domain part of the SUBMITTER address and validate whether the connecting client is authorized to send mail for that domain. If validation fails, the server MUST reject with error 550 5.7.1. The server MUST also verify that the address in the SUBMITTER parameter matches the one found by examining the message headers; if it does not, it MUST reject with 550 5.7.1.

Importantly, the SUBMITTER parameter does not change the reverse-path used for delivery status notifications, nor does it affect reply addresses. When forwarding to a server that does not support SUBMITTER, the forwarding MTA must send the message without the parameter.
sections.plainLanguage: The client puts the submitter's address in the MAIL command. The server checks if that address's domain really authorized this client to send. If there is a mismatch with the headers, the message is rejected.

sections.title: Real-World Scenarios
sections.content:
A user submitting email through an ISP's submission server provides their own address as the SUBMITTER. When a mail server forwards a message from one user to another, it updates the SUBMITTER to the forwarding user's address and adds Resent-From headers to match.

For a mobile user sending through a carrier network but listing their office address in the From header, the SUBMITTER might be the carrier's address. For a guest using a hotel's email facilities, the SUBMITTER might be a generic guest services account at the hotel's domain. Non-delivery reports also use SUBMITTER to identify who is responsible for the error notification.
sections.plainLanguage: If Alice sends mail through her ISP, the SUBMITTER is her ISP account. If a mailing list forwards her message, the SUBMITTER becomes the mailing list's address instead.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The SUBMITTER parameter can be forged by an attacker, and receiving servers cannot rely on it alone to authenticate a message. Rather, the parameter provides information that allows servers to efficiently validate the sender without downloading the entire message body first.

Receiving servers MUST verify the SUBMITTER parameter against the RFC 2822 headers to prevent attackers from trivially defeating the validation. The SUBMITTER parameter does not authenticate the message itself; it only helps identify the responsible domain for further validation using other mechanisms, such as Sender ID or SPF.
sections.plainLanguage: A bad person could lie about the SUBMITTER, so servers must double-check by looking at the headers too. This rule is meant to help catch spoofing faster, not to prove the email is real all by itself.
